title: Christian vocabulary

objectives.can: Give the classical sense and the Christian use of ecclesia, baptismus, gratia, fides, caritas, salus, sacramentum, peccatum, gloria, spiritus, verbum and iustitia.

explanation.summary: A small group of Latin nouns carries much of the weight of Christian Latin: *ecclesia*, *gratia*, *fides*, *sacramentum*, *spiritus*, *verbum* and their companions. Most were ordinary words first, or borrowed Greek ones, and the Church gave them new work. This lesson sets out each word's classical sense and its Christian use, as history, without deciding any question of doctrine.

sections.heading: Three kinds of Christian word
body: The first Latin Christians had to speak about things for which Latin had no ready vocabulary. They did it in three ways. They took Greek words over whole: *ecclesia*, *baptismus*, *angelus*, *evangelium*, *episcopus* and *presbyter* all come from Greek. They gave old Latin words a new sense: *gratia*, *fides*, *salus*, *sacramentum*, *saeculum* and *virtus* were Latin before the Church used them. And they made new words, of which *salvator* is the clearest.

Behind most of these choices stands the Greek of the New Testament, and behind that, often, a Hebrew word. When the Latin Bible was made, one Latin word was set against a Greek word, and from then on the Latin word carried both its own history and the Greek word's. That is why a Latin word can mean something in the Vulgate that a Roman of Cicero's time would not have expected.

sections.heading: Twelve words at a glance
body: The table gives, for each headword, its older Latin sense, its use in the Vulgate and the Fathers, and a verse to see it in. The 'Christian use' column describes how writers used the word. It does not settle what any of these things is, and later technical definitions are not read back into earlier texts.

A note on spelling. The Vulgate in this library prints *v*, *j* and the ligature of *a* and *e*, so the headword *iustitia* appears there as *justitiam*. The Fathers' texts print *u* for consonantal *v*, so *verbum* appears as *uerbum*. They are the same words.

head: Word
Older Latin sense
Christian use
Where to see it
rows: *ecclesia*
Not a native Latin word: a Greek loan for the assembly of a Greek city, and rare in Latin of the classical period.
The assembly of believers, whether one congregation or the whole body of Christians; the Vulgate also uses it for the assembled people of Israel.
Matthew 16:18; 1 Corinthians 14:34; Ephesians 5:32
*baptismus*
Not a native Latin word: from the Greek verb for dipping or washing. There was no Latin word for it.

The rite of washing with water into the Christian community; also used of other 'washings'. The Vulgate has both the masculine *baptismus* (Matthew 21:25) and the neuter *baptisma* (Acts 1:22, Hebrews 6:2).
Matthew 21:25; Acts 1:22; Hebrews 6:2
*gratia*
Favour, goodwill, charm, and thanks: *gratias* agere is 'to give thanks'.
God's favour and gift, rendering the Greek word charis. In Augustine it becomes a main subject of argument.
Ephesians 2:8; John 1:14, 1:16
*fides*
Trust, reliability, good faith, a promise kept, credit.
Trust in God and belief in what is taught; later also 'the faith', the body of teaching; rendering the Greek pistis.
Hebrews 11:1; 1 Corinthians 13:13
*caritas*
From *carus*, 'dear': affection, esteem; also high price.
Love, rendering the Greek agape. 'Charity' in the Douay translation means love here, not almsgiving.
1 Corinthians 13:13
*salus*
Health, safety, welfare; also a greeting, a wish for someone's good.
Rescue and salvation by God, rendering Hebrew and Greek words for deliverance.
Psalm 26:1; Cyprian, On the Lord's Prayer 1
*sacramentum*
A sum deposited by parties to a lawsuit; the soldier's oath of allegiance; hence a solemn pledge.
In the Vulgate it renders the Greek mysterion, 'secret, mystery'. The Fathers apply it to rites, among them baptism; its narrower technical sense is later.
Ephesians 5:32; Tertullian, On Baptism 1
*peccatum*
A fault, a mistake, a wrong step; the verb *peccare* is 'to stumble, to err'.
Sin: an offence against God, singular or plural; the standard Latin word in the Vulgate.
John 1:29; Psalm 50:6
*gloria*
Fame, renown, credit; also boasting.
The splendour and majesty of God, and the honour given to God; rendering Greek doxa and Hebrew kavod.
Luke 2:14; John 1:14
*spiritus*
Breath, breathing, wind, air; also spirit, courage, pride.
The Spirit of God; also the human spirit. Hebrew ruach and Greek pneuma also mean wind or breath, and the Latin word keeps that range.
Genesis 1:2; John 4:24
*verbum*
A word, an expression, a saying.
Also the Word of John 1, rendering the Greek logos; 'the word of God' as message. Some writers chose *sermo* for logos instead.
John 1:1, 1:14; Cyprian, On the Lord's Prayer 1
*iustitia*
Justice, fairness, equity; a virtue of public life.
Righteousness: being in the right before God, rendering Greek dikaiosyne and Hebrew tsedaqah. The Douay English renders it 'justice'.
Matthew 5:6

sections.heading: Reading a word in its verse
body: None of these words has one meaning. In the Vulgate *spiritus* can be the wind, a breath, a person's spirit or the Spirit of God, and only the sentence decides. *gratia* still means 'thanks' in the phrase *gratias agere*, long after it also means God's favour. When you meet one of the twelve, ask first what the older Latin sense would make of the sentence, then whether the Christian use fits better.

Greek helps with the Vulgate but not always. One Greek word may be rendered by several Latin words, and one Latin word may stand for several Greek ones. The Gospel prologue puts *Verbum* for the Greek logos, while Cyprian, writing of the same person, has *Dei sermo*. Both are good Latin; they show two translators' choices.

sections.heading: New words and borrowed ones
body: *angelus* and *evangelium* are loans that Latin kept almost unchanged. *angelus* is 'messenger' in Greek and Latin alike, and the Christian sense, a messenger of God, is one of its uses. *evangelium* is the 'good news'; the verb *evangelizo* in Luke 2:10 is the same word turned into a Latin verb.

*salvator* is a Christian formation on *salvo*, 'to save'. *episcopus* ('overseer') and *presbyter* ('elder') name offices; both are loans. *saeculum* is 'a generation, an age' in older Latin and comes to mean 'this age, this world', and in phrases such as *in saecula saeculorum* 'for ever'. *virtus* means 'manliness, excellence' and, in the Vulgate, often 'power'.

misunderstandings: Reading a later technical definition back into an earlier text. When Tertullian calls baptism a *sacramentum*, he is using a word with a wider range than the narrower sense the word later has.
Assuming the older sense disappears. *gratia* as 'thanks', *spiritus* as 'wind' and *verbum* as 'word' are as good in the Vulgate as in Cicero.
Treating a word and its English cousin as the same. *caritas* is not 'charity' in the sense of giving to the poor, and *iustitia* in Matthew 5:6 is not only courtroom justice.
Taking the Christian sense from the dictionary's first gloss. Dictionaries list classical senses first, so the first gloss of a word like *caritas* or *gloria* may not be the sense in your verse.

deeper.heading: A language short of a word
body: Cicero remarks that Latin has no single word for the Greek soter, 'saviour'. *salvator* fills that gap, and Christian writers made it the regular word. It shows the second way a language takes in a new idea: not by borrowing, but by building a new word from its own parts.

deeper.heading: Why Greek behind Latin matters
body: The Christian senses of *gratia*, *fides*, *caritas*, *sacramentum*, *gloria*, *spiritus*, *verbum* and *iustitia* are not Latin inventions. They answer to Greek words (charis, pistis, agape, mysterion, doxa, pneuma, logos, dikaiosyne), and the Greek words answer, often, to Hebrew ones. A Latin reader who knows this reads the Vulgate with a second set of associations that Cicero's readers did not have.

examples.analysis: *Ecclesiam* is accusative singular feminine, the object of *aedificabo*: 'I will build my church'. The word is a Greek loan for 'assembly' and here names the community of believers. In the Vulgate it is the usual Latin form of the Greek ekklesia.

quoted.title: Ephesians
quoted.english: For by grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God;
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *Gratia* is in the ablative: 'by grace'. The older senses of *gratia* are favour and goodwill; here the favour is God's, and the verse goes on to call it a gift. The verse goes on to name *fides* as the means: by grace, through faith.

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: The psalm of David before he was anointed. The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life: of whom shall I be afraid?

examples.analysis: *salus* is nominative, a second predicate beside *illuminatio*: 'The Lord is my light and my salvation'. In older Latin the word means health or safety; the Psalm's context is deliverance from enemies, and the Latin word covers both bodily safety and rescue by God.

quoted.title: Matthew
quoted.english: Blessed are they that hunger and thirst after justice: for they shall have their fill.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *justitiam* is the headword *iustitia* in the accusative singular, the object of *esuriunt* and *sitiunt*. The verbs of hunger and thirst take an object here: people long for righteousness. Roman writers use *iustitia* for fair dealing between persons; the Vulgate uses it also for being in the right before God.

examples.analysis: *Spiritus* heads the verse and *spiritu* is the ablative after *in*: 'in spirit'. Latin *spiritus* is first of all breath or wind. The Gospel's Greek word pneuma has the same range, which is why the same Latin word is used in this verse for what God is and for how God is worshipped.
